We discuss the problem of a possible remagnetization but consider that this direction of magnetization gives a good approximation for the palaeolatitude of the Lhasa block during Middle to late Cretaceous time. Results from more recent Tibetan formations are also presented: late Cretaceous to Palaeocene sediments and volcanics give a lower palaeolatitude of 10"N and but more recent andesites have emplaced about 30"N, close to the present-day latitude. An interpretation is proposed whereby the Lhasa block, which was a part of Asia in the early Cretaceous, has undergone first a southward motion accompanied by an anticlockwise rotation and then, after the Palaeocene, a northwar

to the Takena formation with a thickness of about 1OOOm. The age of this series spans from Albian-Cenonianian at the base to an unknown age at the top. The Gangdise plutonic belt intrudes the folded Mesozoic series. The folded Takena and older formations are overlain unconformably by red conglomerates with an intercalation of tuffs and thick volcanics (Lingzizong formation). The Breggia gorge (Ticino, Switzerland) provides a continuous outcrop of Mesozoic limestones covering the time between the Lower Jurassic and Upper Cretaceous. The Jurassic section from the Lower Pliens- bachian to Aalenian is well dated by ammonites. The limestones of these stages are a good quality recorder of the polarity of the geomagnetic field during this time interval. More than 500 cores have been drilled along a 120m thick section with a median distance between cores of about 20cm. Detailed thermal and af demagnetization and further rock magnetic studies were used to determine the characteristic NRM direction for each sample. Initial NRM intensities and low field susceptibilities reflect variations in oxidation potential and sedimentation rate during carbonate deposition. The Breggia section covers an estimated 12 Myr of Lower to Middle Jurassic time during which more than 60 distinct reversals of the geomagnetic field are recorded. This corresponds to a comparatively high mean reversal frequency of about 5 reversals Myr-’. The Breggia polarity zonation can be correlated with the nearby section at Alpe Turati (Como, Italy) and comparable polarity pat

cy of about 5 reversals Myr-’. Introduction The development of cryogenic and digital fluxgate magnetometers, which allow rapid and accurate measurement of weakly magnetized rock sequences such as limestones or deep-sea sediments, has resulted in a proliferation of magnetostratigraphic investigations. Many of these studies have concentrated on Late Cretaceous or Palaeogene strata (e.g. Lowrie & Alvarez 1977; LaBrecque et al. 1981 ; Lowrie et al. 1982) and excellent correlation between magnetostratigraphic polarity intervals and Cainozoic marine magnetic anomalies has been obtained. However, the correlation of the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous ‘M-sequence’ of marine anomalies (Larson & Pitman 1972) and the significance and duration of the Jurassic magnetic quiet interval is not so clear-cut. The dating of the beginning and end of the M-sequence of oceanic anomalies is still imprecise. Larson & Hilde (1975) estimated the age of the oldest M-anomalies at about 153 Myr on the basis of basal sediment ages in 706 DSDP hole

nsive viscous remagnetization (Lowrie &Kent 1978). Detailed palaeomagnetic studies of continuously deposited Jurassic sections now exposed on land may establish the nature of the Jurassic quiet zone and also set time constraints on its duration. McElhinny & Burek (1971) concluded on the basis of the available data that normal geomagnetic polarity predominated during the Jurassic with a mixed polarity interval starting at about the Oxfordian/Kimmeridgian boundary. Although this picture was not very accurate because of the poor stratigraphic control of the data used, it did not change appre- ciably for some time (Creer 1971 ; Johnson, Nairn & Peterson 1972; Pechersky & Khramov 1973 ; Irving & Pullaiah 1976). It is usually difficult to obtain accurate age control in continental deposits, but high quality biostratigraphic zonation is often found in marine limestone sequences. Polarity patterns derived from Late Jurassic limestone sequences in the Southern Alps (Ogg 1981; Channell, Ogg & Lowrie 1982a) suggest that the oldest of the M-sequence anomalies (M-25) has an age close to the Oxfordian/Kimmeridgian boundary. Oxfordian limestones in Franconia (Southern Germany) are normally magnetized (Heller 1977). A Lower Jurassic Pliensbachian pelagic limestone section from Hunga

These limestones correspond litho- and biostratigraphically (Wiedenmayer 1980) to the Morbio member of the Breggia section. The Jurassic section from the Lower Pliens- bachian to Aalenian is well dated by ammonites. The limestones of these stages are a good quality recorder of the polarity of the geomagnetic field during this time interval. More than 500 cores have been drilled along a 120m thick section with a median distance between cores of about 20cm. Detailed thermal and af demagnetization and further rock magnetic studies were used to determine the characteristic NRM direction for each sample. Initial NRM intensities and low field susceptibilities reflect variations in oxidation potential and sedimentation rate during carbonate deposition. Introduction The development of cryogenic and digital fluxgate magnetometers, which allow rapid and accurate measurement of weakly magnetized rock sequences such as limestones or deep-sea sediments, has resulted in a proliferation of magnetostratigraphic investigations. Many of these studies have concentrated on Late Cretaceous or Palaeogene strata (e.g. Lowrie & Alvarez 1977; LaBrecque et al. 1981 ; Lowrie et al. 1982) and excellent correlation between magnetostratigraphic polarity intervals and Cainozoic marine magnetic anomalies has been obtained. However, the correlation of the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous ‘M-sequence’ of marine anomalies (Larson & Pitman 1972) and the significance and duration of the Jurassic magnetic quiet interval is not so clear-cut. The dating of the beginning and end of the M-sequence of oceanic anomalies is still imprecise. Larson & Hilde (1975) estimated the age of the oldest M-anomalies at about 153 Myr on the basis of basal sediment ages in 706 DSDP holes. The lack of prominent oceanic magnetic lineations older than this time limit defines a Jurassic magnetic quiet zone which

Geological setting and sampling The Cab0 de Penas region lies on the North Coast of Spain where the northern limb of the Asturian arc is truncated by the sea. In the cliffs from Cab0 de Penas towards the south- east (Fig. 1) an almost complete succession exists from Lower Ordovician till Lower Carboniferous (Truyols & Julivert 1976). The ‘Barrios’ quartzite is overlain by Ordovician shales, with an intercalation of volcanic material in the lower part. Above, the Ordovician ’ series end up with a volcano-detritic succession, including basaltic lavas in the upper part. Then, there is an uninterrupted period of sedimentation up to Early Carboniferous times, with large amounts of fossils giving well-determined stratigraphical ages. Several periods of red sedimentation occur in the sequence. In particular the Siluro-Devonian ‘Furada’ sandstone (called San Pedro elsewhere) is associated with iron ores and has not been sampled because it is unlikely that these complex ores will yield usful palaeomagnetic information. The whole area has been folded by Hercynian deformation and has a general NE-SW trending synclinal shape. Locally, the strata are strongly deformed (Julivert 1976)

Late Devonian-Early Carboniferous sedimentary samples reveal a pre- or syntectonic Carboniferous remanent magnetization similar to the secondary one of the volcanic samples. A soft post-tectonic component appears also in few samples, for which a Late Carboniferous age is inferred. Comparison of the Carboniferous remanent magnetizations and structural parameters suggests that in a late stage of the deformation, the sites have undergone minor rotations around a vertical axis. A 'strike correction' is therefore proposed to take such an effect into account. The average of the corrected mean-site directions (D = 178", I= 19', og5 = 9") is considered to be a good approximation of the Early or Middle Carboniferous palaeomagnetic direction in Asturia. Geological setting and sampling The Cab0 de Penas region lies on the North Coast of Spain where the northern limb of the Asturian arc is truncated by the sea. In the cliffs from Cab0 de Penas towards the south- east (Fig. 1) an almost complete succession exists from Lower Ordovician till Lower Carboniferous (Truyols & Julivert 1976). The ‘Barrios’ quartzite is overlain by Ordovician shales, with an intercalation of volcanic material in the lower part. Above, the Ordovician ’ series end up with a volcano-detritic succession, including basaltic lavas in the upper part. Then, there is an uninterrupted period of sedimentation up to Early Carboniferous times, with large amounts of fossils giving well-determined stratigraphical ages. Several periods of red sedimentation occur in the sequence. In particular the Siluro-Devonian ‘Furada’ sandstone (called San Pedro elsewhere) is associated with iron ores and has not been sampled because it is unlikely that these complex ores will yield usful palaeomagnetic information. The whole area has been folded by Hercynian deformation and has a general NE-SW trending synclinal shape. Locally, the strata are strongly deformed (Julivert 1976)

The Assynt district is centred on a series of thrusted Cambrian sediments between the Lewisian fore- land to the west and the Moine schists to the east. The Assynt igneous suite comprises two major intrusions, the Borrolan and Loch Ailsh centres (Fig. l), and a complex of dykes and sills. The Assynt district is centred on a series of thrusted Cambrian sediments between the Lewisian fore- land to the west and the Moine schists to the east. The Assynt igneous suite comprises two major intrusions, the Borrolan and Loch Ailsh centres (Fig. l), and a complex of dykes and sills. The Ben Loyal igneous complex lies some 30 km north of Assynt and intrudes Moine metasediments. Exposure is poor, especially of the outer phases, for which sampling was limited to the river sections, a quarry and isolated exposures in the peaty lowland. A total of 21 sites were drilled, of which 10 were in the inner phase (Fig. 2). The Loch Ailsh intrusion consists of a variety of broadly uniform leuco-syenites which are well exposed, and a total of six sites were drilled. Lamprophyric dykes and sills exposed along the road and along the shore of Loch Assynt, north of Borrolan, were sampled at nine sites. The Achmelvich dyke was sampled at the coast near Lochinver. It is petrographically similar to ledmorite suggesting a common mag matic origin (Sabine 1953). The Ben Loyal syenite complex comprises three distinct centres of varying grain size and composition. The coarse rock of Ben Loyal itself was sampled at one site, eight sites were drilled in the finer-grained, most mafic Cnoc nan Cuilean intrusion, including two sites in cross-cutting aplite dykes. It is possible (but unlikely) that the palaeomagnetic direction corresponds to a later, post-thrust remagnetization rather than to the original cooling of the body. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have been recognized. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. The data emphasize previously p

these British Ordovician-Silurian data and the contemporary North American data on conventional north Atlantic reconstructions (e.g. Bullard, Everett & Smith 1965) suggesting that an even larger tectonic discontinuity existed between Britain and the North American craton margin. Van der Voo & Scotese (1982) have argued that large (- 2000km) post-Caledonian movement along the Great Glen Fault could account for these discrepancies. Further, in the Devonian the British data are not only discordant with North American data, but also with those from the Baltic region. As a contribution to the enhancement of the database, which is a prerequisite to the solution of these problems, intrusive rocks in the thrust belt marginal to the deformed Caledonides and adjacent to the stable foreland have been studied palaeomagnetically and the results are reported in this paper. They have all been regarded as of Ordovician age although direct evidence of this is only available for some of them. Figure 1. Distribution of the major alkaline intrusions in NW Scotland. The major nappes are also shown (after Parsons 1972). Briden Department ofEurth Sciences, University of Leeds, Leeds LS2 9JT Received 1983 February 28; in original form 1982 October 1 I Summary. A detailed thermal demagnetization study has been carried out on a number of syenitic intrusions from north of the Great Glen Fault in Scotland. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have been recognized. These define a series of palaeomagnetic poles from which an Ordovician to Silurian apparent polar wander path for northern Scotland is deduced. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. The Assynt district is centred on a series of thrusted Cambrian sediments between the Lewisian fore- land to the west and the Moine schists to the east. The Assynt igneous suite comprises two major intrusions, the Borrolan and Loch Ailsh centres (Fig. l), and a complex of dykes and sills. The Ben Loyal igneous complex lies some 30 km north of Assynt and intrudes Moine metasediments. Additionally, a small collection was made from the Achmelvich dyke intruding Lewisian gneisses on the stable Caledonian foreland some 20 km west of Assynt. The multicomponent remanences found in these rocks will be discussed in relation to the timing and scale of local thrusting as well as in relation to the larger scale plate movements associated with Caledonian orogenesis. 2 Geology Almost all the successful palaeomagnetic studies on the Scottish Lower Palaeozoic have been made on dioritic, andesitic, basaltic and ultrabasic igneous rocks. Many of the more acid rocks are palaeomagnetically unstable, e.g. Newer Granites of Garabal Hill (Briden 1970) and Criffel-Dalbeattie (S. J. Kneen, unpublished data). The subjects of the present study are mainly alkaline intrusive rocks, although composition varies considerably within and between the complexes. Chemical and isotopic age data suggest a genetic relationship to the Newer Granite suite (Turnell 1982). The Sole, Ben More, Glencoul and Assynt thrusts form an imbricate series which youngs to the west (Elliot & Johnson 1980). The Moine Thrust overrides the other nappes from the east and it may be that this difference in geometry of the Moine nappe is related to the Assynt intrusions having already been emplaced in the imbricate pile. Briden Department ofEurth Sciences, University of Leeds, Leeds LS2 9JT Received 1983 February 28; in original form 1982 October 1 I Summary. A detailed thermal demagnetization study has been carried out on a number of syenitic intrusions from north of the Great Glen Fault in Scotland. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have been recognized. These define a series of palaeomagnetic poles from which an Ordovician to Silurian apparent polar wander path for northern Scotland is deduced. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. The data emphasize previously published discrepancies between the apparent polar wander paths of Britain, Baltica and Laurentia and are con- sistent with the suggestion that Britain was among a set of intracratonic microplates which underwent complicated, distinct movements throughout the Caledonian orogeny. 1 Introduction

A detailed thermal demagnetization study has been carried out on a number of syenitic intrusions from north of the Great Glen Fault in Scotland. Multicomponent remanences of normal and reversed polarity have been recognized. These define a series of palaeomagnetic poles from which an Ordovician to Silurian apparent polar wander path for northern Scotland is deduced. Comparison of this apparent polar wander path with the estab- lished path for Britain throws new light on the sequence of thrusting and magmatic activity in the NW Highlands and precludes large-scale (5 1500 km) movement along the Great Glen Fault later than the Ordovician. Exposure is poor, especially of the outer phases, for which sampling was limited to the river sections, a quarry and isolated exposures in the peaty lowland. A total of 21 sites were drilled, of which 10 were in the inner phase (Fig. 2). The Loch Ailsh intrusion consists of a variety of broadly uniform leuco-syenites which are well exposed, and a total of six sites were drilled. Lamprophyric dykes and sills exposed along the road and along the shore of Loch Assynt, north of Borrolan, were sampled at nine sites. The Achmelvich dyke was sampled at the coast near Lochinver. It is petrographically similar to ledmorite suggesting a common mag matic origin (Sabine 1953). The Ben Loyal syenite complex comprises three distinct centres of varying grain size and composition. 1978a, b, 1979a, b, 1980a) established an apparent polar wander path (apwp) for this part of Europe. This Armorican apwp is one constraint on tectonic models of orogenies such as the Cadomain, Taconic, Caledonian, Acadian and the Hercynian of Late Precambrian and Palaeozoic times which border the Atlantic realm. Although much has been accomplished in relatively few years, the palaeomagnetic record for these times is still just emerging. Polarity ambiguities combined with rapid Precambrian apparent polar wander, dating inaccuracies and a general scarcity of palaeomagnetic data, result in apwp's with a variety of interpretations (McWilliams 1980). To overcome this problem, more high quality data must be collected to both fill gaps in and substantiate the palaeomagnetic record. This study, as part of the cooperative project, was initiated to document the Armorican apwp further and reports palaeomagnetic results from Late Precambrian and Cambrian igneous rocks (time-scale of Van Eysinga 1975) from the 'Armorican Massif. Two lithologies were sampled; the keratophyre tuffs of Trdguier (640 2 12 Myr) and the microgranite dykes of Loguivy (548 2 24Myr) both dated by whole rock Rb-Sr isochrons recalculated with X = 1.42 x 10-"yr-' from Vidal (1976). About 160 samples of keratophyre tuffs were collected at 19 sites (eight sites near Treguier and 11 sites near Porz Even in the east, Fig. Ic). Nearly all of the keratophyre samples were collected in the field as drilled cores by A. Dubos and N. Bonhommet (Rennes) and 11. Van der Voo. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: 1978a, b, 1979a, b, 1980a) established an apparent polar wander path (apwp) for this part of Europe. This Armorican apwp is one constraint on tectonic models of orogenies such as the Cadomain, Taconic, Caledonian, Acadian and the Hercynian of Late Precambrian and Palaeozoic times which border the Atlantic realm. Although much has been accomplished in relatively few years, the palaeomagnetic record for these times is still just emerging. Polarity ambiguities combined with rapid Precambrian apparent polar wander, dating inaccuracies and a general scarcity of palaeomagnetic data, result in apwp's with a variety of interpretations (McWilliams 1980). To overcome this problem, more high quality data must be collected to both fill gaps in and substantiate the palaeomagnetic record. This study, as part of the cooperative project, was initiated to document the Armorican apwp further and reports palaeomagnetic results from Late Precambrian and Cambrian igneous rocks (time-scale of Van Eysinga 1975) from the 'Armorican Massif. Two lithologies were sampled; the keratophyre tuffs of Trdguier (640 2 12 Myr) and the microgranite dykes of Loguivy (548 2 24Myr) both dated by whole rock Rb-Sr isochrons recalculated with X = 1.42 x 10-"yr-' from Vidal (1976). In contrast, the microgranite high-intensity directions show more scatter both between and within sites than the low intensity group, and the high intensity directions show polarity reversals; occasionally even within the same sample (Fig. 10c). Also the decay of the high intensity remanence during demagnetization differs from that of the low intensity group (Fig. 1 lb, c). Low intensity samples have little relative intensity decay at temperatures below 200°C. At higher temperatures the remanence decays at a fairly constant rate as the Curie temperature of magnetite is approached. High intensity samples on the other hand, have large relative intensity drops at temperatures below 200°C and the remanence decay rate varies greatly at different temperatures. The normalized intensity decays rapidly at lower temperatures; then reaches a 'plateau' at intermediate levels, and finally decays rapidly again at temperatures >500°C. Combined with the much steeper high intensity mean direction (200°/50.8"), the above traits indicate a fundamental difference between the two microgranite dyke magnetizations. Samples of the keratophyre tuffs of Trkguier (640 ? 12 Myr) of the Upper Brioverian series, and the microgranite dykes of Loguivy (548 k 24 Myr) have been collected from the north coast of Brittany, France. ian and Palaeozoic times which border the Atlantic realm. Although much has been accomplished in relatively few years, the palaeomagnetic record for these times is still just emerging. Polarity ambiguities combined with rapid Precambrian apparent polar wander, dating inaccuracies and a general scarcity of palaeomagnetic data, result in apwp's with a variety of interpretations (McWilliams 1980). Two late Mesozoic dolerite sills, situated near Agardhbukta on the east coast of Vestspitsbergen and dated radiometrically at 100 k 4 Myr BP, have been sampled in five localities and subjected to detailed mineralogical and rock magnetic studies to determine the direction and origin of their magnetization. Although the sills lie outside the Tertiary orogenic belt, one locality (no. 4) has undergone strong hydrothermal alteration and a small part of another locality (no. 3) has also been affected. A conventional pro- cedure based on examination of Zijderveld diagrams, applied to specimens demagnetized by alternating fields and thermally, yielded similar remanence directions at all five localities, except at the altered part of locality 3. Using a least squares computer method of analysis of step demagnetization data, comparable directions were isolated from all localities, including the altered part of locality 3. Except in this last case, all directions were reversed. her gabbro bodies. They noted in particular that the mean direction from the Boganclogh mass was very different from the Insch mass. This presented a problem as the Boganclogh mass is an extension of the Insch mass, the link between them being buried beneath a veneer of Old Red Sandstone. her gabbro bodies. They noted in particular that the mean direction from the Boganclogh mass was very different from the Insch mass. This presented a problem as the Boganclogh mass is an extension of the Insch mass, the link between them being buried beneath a veneer of Old Red Sandstone. With this reservation, they computed the total mean direction of magnetization for the Newer Gabbros and an often-quoted early Ordovician pole position. Carmichael & Storetvedt (1981) sought to refute the suggestion that this mean direction of magnetization is truly representative of the palaeomagnetic record of the gabbro. They pointed out that the demagnetization techniques employed by Sallomy & Piper (1973) may not have been sufficiently rigorous fully to reveal the potentially multivectorial nature of the magnetization of these rocks. her gabbro bodies. They noted in particular that the mean direction from the Boganclogh mass was very different from the Insch mass. This presented a problem as the Boganclogh mass is an extension of the Insch mass, the link between them being buried beneath a veneer of Old Red Sandstone. Remanent magnetization directions of 32 dykes and lava flows sampled near Ayacucho, the Peruvian Andes revealed 14.2' f 5.5" counter- clockwise rotation after the Neogene intrusion of this dyke swarm. Palaeo- magnetic results of these rocks and other palaeomagnetic evidences from the Central Andean Mesozoic rocks suggest relatively recent occurrence of the Andean oroclinal bending around the axis at the Peru-Chile border. Introduction Palaeomagnetic studies on the Mesozoic rocks of the Peruvian Andes and northernmost Chile (Heki, Hamano & Kono 1983; Heki 1983; Heki et al. 1984) have revealed post-Cretaceous counter-clockwise rotation of the Peruvian block and oroclinal bending

Chile border. Introduction Palaeomagnetic studies on the Mesozoic rocks of the Peruvian Andes and northernmost Chile (Heki, Hamano & Kono 1983; Heki 1983; Heki et al. 1984) have revealed post-Cretaceous counter-clockwise rotation of the Peruvian block and oroclinal bending of the Central Andes around an axis at the Peru-Chile border (referred to as the Bolivian orocline; Carey 1955). Hayashida er al. (1 984) also showed the counter-clockwise deviated declination of the Eocene red sediments of the Salla Group in the Bolivian Altiplano and suggested that the oroclinal bending is post-Eocene. Palaeomagnetic studies for much younger rock formations will provide important information on the age of the bending of the Central Andes. Here we report the result of a palaeomagnetic investigation on a Neogene dyke swarm near Ayacucho, in the Peruvian Andes. bout an order of magnitude lower than estimated cooling rates in the Alps over the past few tens of million years (Baer 1981a). For this reason, and because of the concentration of 1100-1 150 Myr old whole-rock Rb/Sr ages in the central part of the Grenville where the structural grain is NNE and oblique to the Grenville Front, Baer favours a compound cooling history with separate thermal events around 1150-1 100 and 950-900 Ma. The Central Metasedimentary Belt containing the Hastings region is one of the areas that should have felt the effects of a penetrative 1150-1 100 Myr event, but the palaeomagnetic data do not bear this out. All palaeopoles so far reported seem to fall in the 1050-820 Myr interval and are very different from 1150-1 100 Ma poles for rocks of the Lake Superior Keweenawan rift sequence (Fig. l), which may be genetically related to the Grenvillian event or events (Donaldson & Irving 1972; Baer 1981 b). The palaeomagnetic observations do not rule out an 1150-1100 Ma event followed by reheating around 1050-1000Ma to a temperature of about 650”6, which would be sufficient to erase all pre-existing magnetization. 40Ar/39Ar stepheating data for the Thanet complex (Berger & York 1981) are compatible with this compound model: one hornblende with an Ar closure tem

by Symons (1978), Irving (1979), Roy & Robertson (1979), Dunlop (1981), Irving & McGlynn (1981) and Park & Emslie (1983). More specialized reviews of the palaeo- magnetism and geochronology of the Hastings-Haliburton region have been given by Dunlop et al. (1980), Dunlop & Schutts (1983) and York (1984). Early studies were aimed at testing two different views of the ‘Tibetan model’ of the Grenville orogen. In the first view, the Grenvillian analogue of the Himalayan collision zone would lie near the southern edge of the Grenville Front Tectonic Zone (Fig. 1) and much of the Grenville would be an exotic terrane, with a pre-collisional apparent polar wander path (APW) different from that of the remainder of Laurentia. In the other view, ‘Grenvillia’ and ‘Interior Laurentia’ form part of a single plate and the collisional zone lies to the SE of both. or hornblendes from the Thanet and Cordova gabbros (Berger & York 1981; Lopez-Martinez & York 1983) intensified the search. Of course, whether a pre-metamorphic magnetization in either of these intrusions would be strictly pre-orogenic depends on whether the Grenvillian collision coincided with the 1150- 1100 Ma event proposed by Baer (1981a) or with the earlier deformational event which predated these intrusions. When a novel C component of magnetization was discovered in the Cordova gabbro (Dunlop et al. 1980), it was suggested on the basis of preliminary results that it might represent a pre-orogenic magnetization, or at any rate a remanence older than any previously uncovered. The detailed results presented in this paper show that this speculation was wrong. The C magnetization is a low-temperature Silurian or late Ordovician overprint, dated at 445-450 Ma by 40Ar/39Ar on plagioclase (Lopez-Martinez & York 1983). This is the first palaeomagnetic evidence for a possible ‘echo’ in the Crenville of Acadian-Caledonian events in the Appalachian Orogen. Field and laboratory procedures One hundred and thirty block samples were collected from 23 sites in the Cordova gabbro (Fig. 2). Samples were oriented by magnetic compass and strike readings were checked 1-2 m above the outc

podal directions (normal or N polarity), as shown in Fig. 4. The ratio of R to N is about 4 to 1. In most cases, the A remanence was revealed only after removal of a magnetization in the PEF direction between 0 and 150Oe or between 20 and 250-300°C. This soft PEF component is presumed to be a room temperature viscous overprint acquired in the Brunhes epoch. A statistical analysis of site mean A magnetization directions appears in Table 1. The N mean is not exactly 180" reversed to the R mean. N is displaced about 10" towards R along a great circle passing through the PEF direction, probably indicating imperfect removal of PEF viscous remanence. The mean A direction for R and N sites combined is D = 294", I = - 55.5", with k = 42 and ag5 = 5.5". Individual samples recorded both an A magnetization with a palaeopole near Australia and a B magnetization with a palaeopole in the equatorial Pacific. The A magnetization was demonstrably older than the B, and the A-B sequence seemed to mark a convergent juncture with the Logan Loop or Keweenawan Track of the Laurentian APWP. The Hastings Lowlands is one of the few parts of the Grenville from which pre-orogenic magnetizations might possibly be recovered. bout an order of magnitude lower than estimated cooling rates in the Alps over the past few tens of million years (Baer 1981a). For this reason, and because of the concentration of 1100-1 150 Myr old whole-rock Rb/Sr ages in the central part of the Grenville where the structural grain is NNE and oblique to the Grenville Front, Baer favours a compound cooling history with separate thermal events around 1150-1 100 and 950-900 Ma. The Central Metasedimentary Belt containing the Hastings region is one of the areas that should have felt the effects of a penetrative 1150-1 100 Myr event, but the palaeomagnetic data do not bear this out. All palaeopoles so far reported seem to fall in the 1050-820 Myr interval and are very different from 1150-1 100 Ma poles for rocks of the Lake Superior Keweenawan rift sequence (Fig. l), which may be genetically related to the Grenvillian event or events (Donaldson & Irving 1972; Baer 1981 b). The palaeomagnetic observations do not rule out an 1150-1100 Ma event followed by reheating around 1050-1000Ma to a temperature of about 650”6, which would be sufficient to erase all pre-existing magnetization. 40Ar/39Ar stepheating data for the Thanet complex (Berger & York 1981) are compatible with this compound model: one hornblende with an Ar closure tem

by Symons (1978), Irving (1979), Roy & Robertson (1979), Dunlop (1981), Irving & McGlynn (1981) and Park & Emslie (1983). More specialized reviews of the palaeo- magnetism and geochronology of the Hastings-Haliburton region have been given by Dunlop et al. (1980), Dunlop & Schutts (1983) and York (1984). Early studies were aimed at testing two different views of the ‘Tibetan model’ of the Grenville orogen. In the first view, the Grenvillian analogue of the Himalayan collision zone would lie near the southern edge of the Grenville Front Tectonic Zone (Fig. 1) and much of the Grenville would be an exotic terrane, with a pre-collisional apparent polar wander path (APW) different from that of the remainder of Laurentia. In the other view, ‘Grenvillia’ and ‘Interior Laurentia’ form part of a single plate and the collisional zone lies to the SE of both. Of course, whether a pre-metamorphic magnetization in either of these intrusions would be strictly pre-orogenic depends on whether the Grenvillian collision coincided with the 1150- 1100 Ma event proposed by Baer (1981a) or with the earlier deformational event which predated these intrusions. When a novel C component of magnetization was discovered in the Cordova gabbro (Dunlop et al. 1980), it was suggested on the basis of preliminary results that it might represent a pre-orogenic magnetization, or at any rate a remanence older than any previously uncovered. The detailed results presented in this paper show that this speculation was wrong. The C magnetization is a low-temperature Silurian or late Ordovician overprint, dated at 445-450 Ma by 40Ar/39Ar on plagioclase (Lopez-Martinez & York 1983). This is the first palaeomagnetic evidence for a possible ‘echo’ in the Crenville of Acadian-Caledonian events in the Appalachian Orogen. For this reason, and because of the concentration of 1100-1 150 Myr old whole-rock Rb/Sr ages in the central part of the Grenville where the structural grain is NNE and oblique to the Grenville Front, Baer favours a compound cooling history with separate thermal events around 1150-1 100 and 950-900 Ma. More specialized reviews of the palaeo- magnetism and geochronology of the Hastings-Haliburton region have been given by Dunlop et al. (1980), Dunlop & Schutts (1983) and York (1984). Received 1984 November 9; in original form 1984 July 23 Summary. The Cordova gabbro of southern Ontario intrudes 1300 Myr old volcanic rocks of the Hastings Lowlands in the Grenville Structural Province. Three distinct vector magnetizations (A, B and C) have been isolated, using a combination of stable endpoints, subtracted vectors from orthogonal vector plots and converging remagnetization circles. The A magnetization, with mean direction D = 294" I = - 55.5" (k = 42, ag5 = 5.5", N= 18 sites), is a high coercivity, high blocking temperature remanence recorded by 49 samples. The B magnetization was isolated in 33 samples and has a mean direction D = 305.5"1= - 1 .5" (k = 24, ag5 = 9.5", N= 11 sites). B has lower coerci- vities and blocking temperatures than A where the two are superimposed. The A and B palaeopoles, 151"E, 10.5"S (dp = 6", dm = 8") and 165.5" E, 24"N (dp = So, dm = 9.5"), fall on the Grenville Track around 900 and 820 Ma respectively. The A and B magnetizations thus date from uplift and cooling following the Grenvillian orogeny. The third magnetization, the C component, has been isolated in 23 samples. I

or hornblendes from the Thanet and Cordova gabbros (Berger & York 1981; Lopez-Martinez & York 1983) intensified the search. Of course, whether a pre-metamorphic magnetization in either of these intrusions would be strictly pre-orogenic depends on whether the Grenvillian collision coincided with the 1150- 1100 Ma event proposed by Baer (1981a) or with the earlier deformational event which predated these intrusions. When a novel C component of magnetization was discovered in the Cordova gabbro (Dunlop et al. 1980), it was suggested on the basis of preliminary results that it might represent a pre-orogenic magnetization, or at any rate a remanence older than any previously uncovered. The detailed results presented in this paper show that this speculation was wrong. The C magnetization is a low-temperature Silurian or late Ordovician overprint, dated at 445-450 Ma by 40Ar/39Ar on plagioclase (Lopez-Martinez & York 1983). This is the first palaeomagnetic evidence for a possible ‘echo’ in the Crenville of Acadian-Caledonian events in the Appalachian Orogen. note Palaeomagnetism and ages of dolerite dykes in Karimnagar District, Andhra Pradesh, India Y. V. Subba Rao and I. V. Radhakrishna Murthy Department of Geophysics, Andhra University, Waltair, Visakhaputnarn 530 003, India Accepted 1985 January 24. Received 1984 December 12; in original form 1983 May 24 Summary. Results of palaeomagnetic investigations of three dolerite dykes in Karimnagar District, Andhra Pradesh, India are reported. The remanent magnetic directions of specimens from one dyke, called A, fall into two groups, one with a positive inclination and the other with a negative inclination, indicating two intrusions. For dykes B and C, the remanent magnetic directions show a negative inclination. The pole positions for all these dykes are close to those for the Gwalior Traps, whose age is 1830L200Myr. It is inferred that these dykes were emplaced over a short span of time around the Gwalior Trap period, which may represent a phase of multiple igneous activity. Introduction It is a common practice to determine the age of rocks by correlating their palaeomagnetic pole positions with the data for formations of known ages. Palaeomagnetic investigations were carried out over three dolerite dykes in Karimnagar district, Andhra Pradesh, India, mainly to substantiate the interpretation of magnetic anomalies over them. The data thus obtained are, however, used to ascertain the palaeomagnetic age of these dykes. Geology, location and sampling The geological map of the area, situated between latitudes 18"20' and 18"30'N and longitudes 79'0' and 79"15'E, is shown in Fig. 1. The area is mostly occupied by grey granitic gneisses and granites which grade into one another. There are three major dolerite dykes, named A, B and C (Fig. l), intruding into the granitic rocks. Magnetic surveys conducted in this area indicate that they run for several kilometres in a N60"E direction (Subba Rao 1974), although they appear as disconnected ridges on the surface. They are 35-100m wide and have a vertical dip. The age of the dolerite dykes has not been determined by any method. Two members of this suite were chosen for palaeomagnetic study in an attempt to refine the apparent polar wander path for Scotland in the Palaeozoic. This paper describes the results of the detailed palaeomagnetic analysis which has been carried out. Thermal and alternating field (af) demagnetization was supplemented by rock magnetic experiments on a limited selection of specimens from each sampling site to help characterize the remanence carriers. These consisted of thin-section observations and the measurement of thermomagnetic and hysteresis properties. Each complex provides an example of the widespread variability in remanence behaviour which may be encountered in a single intrusion. For an accurate interpretation of palaeomagnetic data from any formation, an estimate of the age of the rock is required. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: gnetism of two complexes from the Newer Granite Suite in Scotland, at Ratagan (NW Highlands) and Comrie (central Highlands), reveals the variable nature of the natural remanence encountered in granodioritic intrusions and the surrounding metamorphic country rock. Forty-eight specimens from Ratagan, dated at 415 Itr 5 Ma, gave a mean direc- tion: D= 8", I= - 32", and a palaeomagnetic south pole: 1S0S, 346"E (6p= 5", Fm=9"). Twenty-eight specimens from Comrie, dated at 40855 Ma, gave a mean direction: D = 75", I= - 30", and a palaeomagnetic south pole: 6"S, 287"E(6p = 4", 6m = 7"). These results have been compared with the established apparent polar wander path (APWP) for Britain. The Ratagan pole improves the reliability of the APWP but doubt remains as to whether the primary magnetization from Comrie represents a true late Silurian direction or whether it has been affected by post-cooling rotation, possibly associated with the nearby Highland Boundary Fault. Key words: palaeomagnetisrn, Palaeozoic intrusions, Rb-Sr ages, Scotland 1 Introduction The newer igneous rocks in the Scottish Highland region which post-date the main Grampian metamorphism and tectonism range in composition from basic to granitic. Two members of this suite were chosen for palaeomagnetic study in an attempt to

e compatible with other known lower Palaeozoic poles from Scotland (e.g. Piper 1979). Therefore, all the data have been combined to produce a single pole position. It was initiated during the late Jurassic or Early Cretaceous at the commencement of rifting between Australia and Antarctica. North Rankin 1 was drilled into a major structural element on the western edge of the Dampier Sub-basin - the Rankin Platform. This platform consists of large fault blocks, which were formed during the mid-Mesozoic extensional phase and have been subsequently draped by sediments. e been carried out on one Cretaceous and five Cenozoic sedimentary sequences of Australia; of those, one is in the Carnarvon Basin of north-western Australia, and the others are in the Otway Basin of south-eastern Australia. The new results are used together with those published previously to define a revised late Mesozoic-Cenozoic apparent polar wander path for Australia. This path differs from earlier, basalt-derived paths by the absence of a large westward excursion and zig-zag irregularities. It is characterized instead by a substantially straight Cenozoic trajectory, a sharp bend in the Late Cretaceous, and a non-uniform rate of apparent polar wander. The early Tertiary segment of the new path lies north of the original paths, thus eliminating a discrepancy that has been noted previously between the Indian and Australian palaeomagnetic data (Luyendyk & Rennick, Peirce and Klootwyk & Peirce). A re-examination of the original data suggests that this discrepancy, as well as two others in the Australian results, may have been caused principally by incomplete time-averaging of remanence directions, because the volcanics on which the results were based had been extruded episodically. In 1970 Wilson pointed out that secular variations are not necessarily cancelled by averaging between successive lava flows, because groups of flows can be extruded over short periods of time. In Wilson's study of Tertiary lavas of Northern Ireland, 32 flows in a sequence of 54 appeared to have been extruded in four brief episodes. Brief periods of basalt extrusion have also been reported from other parts of the world, such as the Stoddart Formation in New Zealand (Evans 1970); Steen Mountains in the USA (Watkins & Baksi 1974); and some Hawaiian lavas (McWilliams, Holcomb & Champion 1982). Most of the Australian Cenozoic poles had been determined by measurements on one principal extinct volcano, supplemented by fewer measurements on other volcanoes. Thus, four out of six poles on the latest basalt-derived path are based primarily on measurements of the Barrington, Liverpool, Nandewar and Tweed volcanoes. The first three of these, like the lavas reported by Wilson (1970), appear to have successive flows with similar remanence directions. In 1970 Wilson pointed out that secular variations are not necessarily cancelled by averaging between successive lava flows, because groups of flows can be extruded over short periods of time. In Wilson's study of Tertiary lavas of Northern Ireland, 32 flows in a sequence of 54 appeared to have been extruded in four brief episodes. Brief periods of basalt extrusion have also been reported from other parts of the world, such as the Stoddart Formation in New Zealand (Evans 1970); Steen Mountains in the USA (Watkins & Baksi 1974); and some Hawaiian lavas (McWilliams, Holcomb & Champion 1982). Most of the Australian Cenozoic poles had been determined by measurements on one principal extinct volcano, supplemented by fewer measurements on other volcanoes. Thus, four out of six poles on the latest basalt-derived path are based primarily on measurements of the Barrington, Liverpool, Nandewar and Tweed volcanoes. The first three of these, like the lavas reported by Wilson (1970), appear to have successive flows with similar remanence directions. In these samples and 27 others like them, the orthogonal vector diagram of thermal demagnetization data is ideal: both vector components define linear segments that intersect sharply between 5 15 and 525°C. Numerous palaeomagnetic poles that were at first believed to ‘see through’ the Grenvillian orogeny almost certainly date from post-meta- morpluc regional uplift and cooling (e.g. Irving, Emslie & Uena 1974; Buchan & Dunlop 1976; Symons 1978). They fall on the Grenville Loop of the Laurentian apparent polar wander path (APWP) in the approximate time interval 1000-800 Ma (Berger, York & Dunlop 1979; Dallmeyer & Sutter 1980). In parts of the Hastings Lowlands of southern Ontario (Fig. l), the metamorpluc grade is unusually low for the Grenville Province and pre-metamorphic 40Ar/39Ar hornblende ages have been recovered. The Jurassic Scisti Silicei Formation forms part of the Lagonegro superimposed tectonic units I and I1 that are thought to represent the axial and internal margins of the Mesozoic Lagonegro Basin, prior to nappe formation. Sampling was carried out in the lower (Lagonegro) and upper (Pignola) nappes in two differently oriented anticlines. Single and multi- component magnetizations are present. Isothermal remanence acquisition rates show that magnetite and haematite are present which, in most hgonegro specimens, show the same direction of magnetization. Comparison of the palaeomagnetic directions with those from Jurassic rocks on the stable African craton indicates a 147" anticlockwise rotation of the lower nappe which is similar to 139" previously reported for the upper nappe at Vietri di Potenza. The same comparisons show a 44" clockwise rotation of the upper nappe at Pignola. These results suggest that the doubled nappe structures, sampled some 50 km apart, resulted from their emplacement by translation with little rotation prior to the ope

carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: conclusions The steep inclinations which predominate in the Lagonegro locality, and are of restricted occurrence in the Pignola area, are well defined and of consistent reversed polarity. This suggests that they were acquired in a reversed geomagnetic field prior to folding. However, such an inclination is inconsistent with any possible post-Triassic palaeolatitude for this area (c. 25-30') or with any direction which could have been acquired during a tilt at some specific time during the nappe development and emplacement. Thus these directions, while clearly defined, remain of unknown origin. The sites from Pignola which show single component magnetization are characterized by a south-westerly declination, intermediate negative inclination, which is carried by magnetite, while the north-westerly direction, of intermediate positive inclination, is characteristic of the high temperature component of the multicomponent sites which contain magnetite, specularite and pigmentary haematite. The identification of the SW component in some of the multicomponent sites, together with the more complex mineralogy, indicates that the NW direction probably represents a later acquired magnetiz- ation than the SW directed component. The structure and petrology of the lavas have been examined by Allwright (1980); the majority (- 80 per cent) of them are basaltic and the remainder are differentiates (hawaiites and mugearites) (Allwright 1980 and private communication). Chemically the lavas of Eigg and Muck are broadly similar to those of the Skye Main Lava Series defined by Thompson, Esson & Dunham (1972) and Mull sequences, though a few are similar to the Preshal Mor and Fairy Bridge magma types of Skye (Allwright 1980). Within the Muck sequence several bands of red material, which are seen to overlie weathered basalt and infill cracks in the upper surface of the underlying flow, provide useful marker horizons. The origin of these 'red beds' is uncertain but they may be altered tuffs originating from an explosive event (Allwright, private communication). In Eigg the most conspicuous horizon is a distinctively coloured flow, the Grey Rock, classified as a mugearite by Allwright (1980). Samples have been taken systematically through the intrusive sequence for the three centres which form the Tertiary central intrusive ring complex. Palaeomagnetic measurements show that all the units are reversely magnetized as are the earlier lavas - an extension of those of Mull and Morvern - which they intrude. This is in contrast to Mull. Skye and Arran, where the igneous sequences have been shown to span at least three polarity intervals, but is similar to Rhum where the only normal units are a few late dykes. Rocks from the Massif de la Serre in the French Jura (latitude: 47.3"N longitude: 5.6"E) belonging to an ignimbritic assemblage dominated by vitrophyric rhyolites, and whose age of formation is probably Permian (Autunian to Saxonian) have been studied by applying thermal and alter- nating field demagnetization. The characteristic magnetization has a mean direction derived from 89 samples of D = 170", I = - 16", k = 26.2", 01~~ = 3" and a corresponding north palaeopole at 41"N, 172"E, AgS = 5". The pole, which is very close to the Permian European poles, can thus be considered as a new contribution. Some samples are found to carry a unique normal polarity magnetization, others carry both normal and reverse polarities. It therefore seems that, similar to Permian series in the USSR, these west European rocks have registered a normal event in the Kiaman interval. From a structural point of view, we may conclude that during the Alpine tectonic phases the Massif de la Serre has not been subjected to substantial rotation. e palaeomagnetic data are needed, particularly from Spitsbergen. After the Caledonian activity and its rejuvenation during the Upper Devonian (Harland 1969; Birkenmajer 1981), Spitsbergen remained tectonically stable until the opening of North Atlantic and Arctic basins, which caused the West Spitsbergen orogeny along the western edge of the island. As the Variscan orogeny hardly affected south Spitsbergen, palaeomagnetic studies may provide data undisturbed by the Variscan activity. Devonian rocks in Spitsbergen occur in two N-S trending grabens exposed in the northern part of the island and in a smaller one in the south. The Old Red Sandstone molasse, of late orogenic origin, was deposited in these grabens. The oldest sediments are in the north of the island and the most widespread deposits belong to the Wood Bay Formation. This formation consists of continental red coloured sandstones with siltstones and shales of Siegenian- Emsian age. There are two main sources of clastics (Friend & Moody-Stuard 1972). Key words: palaeomagnetism, K-Ar ages, Cretaceous, Portugal, tectono- magmatic implications Introduction Post-Hercynian palaeomagnetic data from Spain and Portugal have traditionally been associated with a counterclockwise rotational opening of the Bay of Biscay (Schwarz 1963; Van Dongen 1967; Girdler 1968; Watluns & Richardson 1968a; Van der Voo 1969; Stauffer & Tarling 197 1 ; Van der Voo & Zijderveld 197 1 ; Storetvedt 1973; Van den Berg 1979), and the Upper Cretaceous has repeatedly been considered as the time during which Iberia detached from the European plate (Van der Voo 1969; Stauffer & Tarling 1971 ; Williams 1975; Van den Berg 1979; Boillot 1984). However, despite the many geophysical and geo- logical studies, the tectonic setting of Iberia is far from clear, and in a recent discussion on the tectonic evolution of the Pyrenees (see McCaig & Wickham 1984) the need for further detailed palaeomagnetic studies of the Cretaceous of Iberia was stressed. The present paper contributes to this task, reporting new palaeomagnetic and radiometric results from the late Cretaceous Sintra and Sines intrusive complexes of W. Portugal as well as giving further details on the palaeomagnetic structure of the Lisbon volcanics. The latter formation has previo

The Sines complex, located some 105 km south-southeast of the Sintra hills (see Fig. 1 a) shows several characteristic features similar to the Sintra massif, i.e. elliptical shape, nearly east-west orientation, sub-volcanic ring-structure (Teixeira 1962; Ribeiro 1979) etc. The major part of the complex lies offshore. The subaerial part is largely covered by Quaternary deposits, the exposed rocks constituting only a narrow littoral section. Both on the north and south side of the complex thermal aureoles have been generated in the adjacent sedimentary rocks, causing various types of thermometamorphism (Canilho 1971). The most important petrographic types are gabbro, diorite and syenite. The complex is cut by numerous dykes of varied composition. Radiometric studies (see below) suggest that the Sines intrusive mass formed contemporaneously with the Cab0 da Roca complex. This seems to fit the hypothesis of Ribeiro (1 979) that the Sines and Sintra intrusions are connected by a common strike-slip fracture. These complexes form part of the late Cretaceous alkaline igneous province of Iberia (Rock 1982). K. M. There is also a dyke net- work, almost exclusively vertical, and a few late stage volcanic vents piercing lava flows. Petrographically, the Lisbon volcanics are mostly composed of basaltic rocks, but hawaiites and mugearites are also present. Coarser grained varieties include ankaramites and ankaratrites, and aphanitic rocks include basanites and basanitoides (Alves et al. 1980). The volcanic complex comprises at least 15 eruptive centres. Their pipes (plugs, necks and breccias) and part of their cones are still visible, forming an almost continuous belt between the Cascais/Oeiras and Mafra/Malveira districts. The present paper contributes to this task, reporting new palaeomagnetic and radiometric results from the late Cretaceous Sintra and Sines intrusive complexes of W. Portugal as well as giving further details on the palaeomagnetic structure of the Lisbon volcanics. The latter formation has previo

The Sines complex, located some 105 km south-southeast of the Sintra hills (see Fig. 1 a) shows several characteristic features similar to the Sintra massif, i.e. elliptical shape, nearly east-west orientation, sub-volcanic ring-structure (Teixeira 1962; Ribeiro 1979) etc. The major part of the complex lies offshore. The subaerial part is largely covered by Quaternary deposits, the exposed rocks constituting only a narrow littoral section. Both on the north and south side of the complex thermal aureoles have been generated in the adjacent sedimentary rocks, causing various types of thermometamorphism (Canilho 1971). The most important petrographic types are gabbro, diorite and syenite. The complex is cut by numerous dykes of varied composition. Radiometric studies (see below) suggest that the Sines intrusive mass formed contemporaneously with the Cab0 da Roca complex. This seems to fit the hypothesis of Ribeiro (1 979) that the Sines and Sintra intrusions are connected by a common strike-slip fracture. These complexes form part of the late Cretaceous alkaline igneous province of Iberia (Rock 1982). K. M. There is also a dyke net- work, almost exclusively vertical, and a few late stage volcanic vents piercing lava flows. Petrographically, the Lisbon volcanics are mostly composed of basaltic rocks, but hawaiites and mugearites are also present. Coarser grained varieties include ankaramites and ankaratrites, and aphanitic rocks include basanites and basanitoides (Alves et al. 1980). The volcanic complex comprises at least 15 eruptive centres. Their pipes (plugs, necks and breccias) and part of their cones are still visible, forming an almost continuous belt between the Cascais/Oeiras and Mafra/Malveira districts. The Sines complex, located some 105 km south-southeast of the Sintra hills (see Fig. 1 a) shows several characteristic features similar to the Sintra massif, i.e. elliptical shape, nearly east-west orientation, sub-volcanic ring-structure (Teixeira 1962; Ribeiro 1979) etc. The major part of the complex lies offshore. The subaerial part is largely covered by Quaternary deposits, the exposed rocks constituting only a narrow littoral section. Both on the north and south side of the complex thermal aureoles have been generated in the adjacent sedimentary rocks, causing various types of thermometamorphism (Canilho 1971). The most important petrographic types are gabbro, diorite and syenite. The complex is cut by numerous dykes of varied composition. Radiometric studies (see below) suggest that the Sines intrusive mass formed contemporaneously with the Cab0 da Roca complex. This seems to fit the hypothesis of Ribeiro (1 979) that the Sines and Sintra intrusions are connected by a common strike-slip fracture. These complexes form part of the late Cretaceous alkaline igneous province of Iberia (Rock 1982). K. M. There is also a dyke net- work, almost exclusively vertical, and a few late stage volcanic vents piercing lava flows. Petrographically, the Lisbon volcanics are mostly composed of basaltic rocks, but hawaiites and mugearites are also present. Coarser grained varieties include ankaramites and ankaratrites, and aphanitic rocks include basanites and basanitoides (Alves et al. 1980). The volcanic complex comprises at least 15 eruptive centres. Their pipes (plugs, necks and breccias) and part of their cones are still visible, forming an almost continuous belt between the Cascais/Oeiras and Mafra/Malveira districts. Portugal), and further details on the palaeomagnetic structure of the Lisbon volcanics are reported. The Sintra complex consists of two main intrusive phases having been emplaced in the Upper Cretaceous at around 90 Ma and 75 Ma respectively. The radiometric results show that the Sines complex formed concurrently with the second Sintra magmatism. The early (main) Sintra pluton has a characteristic magnetization of D=358', I = 27' (ag5 = 3.3'). If this is the case, the characteristic magnetization is secondary and has replaced any initial magnetization. The mechanism by which the igneous body could have acquired the secondary magnet- ization is difficult to explain, as the overlying red beds, 700 m above, were not affected by late Hadrynian-Cambrian re- magnetization. The thermal demagnetization curves for the igneous rock (Figure 1) show the highest blocking temper- atures to be near 560øC for the carriers of the characteristic magnetization, suggesting that magnetite is the dominant car- rier. A possibility which cannot be excluded is that the characteristic direction of the igneous body (Figure 2) is not one of a single remanence vector but rather the resultant of the decay of two vectors of equal coercivity spectra. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: in and Bays Formations agree very well and indicate a pole position intermediate between the Late Cambrian poles and the cluster of previously published Ordovician poles. The characteristic directions from the Chapman Ridge Formation give a pole located in the cluster of poles at 35øN, 120øE, agreeing very well with the results from the Upper Ordovician Juniata Formation. This may be the result of a remagnetization of the Chapman Ridge Formation or perhaps a hitherto undefined loop occurs in the Ordovician North American polar wander path. Relative rotations between the various sampling sites are a rather remote possibility. A secondary magnetization of the Moccasin Formation is revealed by intermediate blocking- temperature directions in many of the specimens. Unfortunately, the fold test is not conclusive for these components because of their absence from a critical outcrop. The pole position obtained from the in situ directions does not correspond to any known North American post- Mississippian pole position, whereas the pole corresponding to the tilt-corrected directions lies near the Carboniferous poles and the Ordo- vician Trenton pole for North America. Because of the indeterminancy of the age of this magne- tization, any discussion on its origin must be speculative. The favored interpretation is that it is a chemical remagnetization, possibly asso- ciated with diagenesis, acquired before the folding of the Moccasin Formation. Acknowledgments.

This included a minimum 107-s time period prior to the measurement of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM). In addition, two cylindrical shields were utilized during the cooling phase of thermal demagnetization, which reduced the residual mag- netic field to no greater than 5 ¾. Alternating field (af) demagnetization was carried out by a 400-Hz decaying field with a two-axis tumbler. Vector endpoints from partial thermal demagnetization are project- ed onto two orthogonal planes. When these end- points display a trend toward the origin, a sin- gle component of magnetization is present. This means that no rotation of the magnetic vector has occurred at increasing temperatures of demagne- tization. However, if a straight line is formed which does not trend to the origin, it indicates at least a two-component remanence with nonover- lapping blocking temperature spectra. Any curved trend of vector endpoints indicates the decay of multiple magnetic components with overlapping blocking spectra. DISCUSSION If we are justified in assuming that the mean paleomagnetic pole (latitude 23.0øN, longitude 188.8øE; a95 -- 11.0 ø) repre- sents the Late Triassic geocentric axial dipole field, then we can infer the tectonic history of southeastern Alaska. Justifica- tion of this assumption requires that the sample sites span enough time to average out geomagnetic secular variation and excursions. We have sampled 12 different basalt flows, each providing a spot reading of the ancient geomagnetic field. Al- though the exact time interval spanned by these 12 flows is unknown, the flows were erupted during at least two polarity intervals. Consistent dual polarity of the data strongly in- dicates dipolar behavior that probably is not biased by secular variation or an excursion. The hypothe- sis that displaced microplates make up the westernmost belts of the northern Cordillera is founded on stratigraphic and biogeographic evidence [Berg et al., 1972; Jones et al., 1972; Churkin and Eberlein, 1977; Monger, 1977] and has been sup- ported by recently obtained palcomagnetic evidence from Pa- leozoic rocks of the Alexander terrane [Van der Voo et al., !980]. The palcomagnetic results reported herein are from Triassic submarine basalt that is stratigraphically the up- permost part of the Alexander terrane on Kupreanof Island. Most of southeastern Alaska lies within the Alexander ter- rane (Figure 1), a 100-km-wide belt extending from the Yu- kon-Alaska border to the south tip of Prince of Wales Island [Berg et al., 1972, 1978]. The terrane consists of Ordovician through Triassic rocks that were deposited near a continental margin or possibly in an island arc. The Alexander terrane is separated from the west edge of the craton, defined as the Rocky Mountain trench, by several belts that include a belt of late Paleozoic oceanic crust. This oceanic terrane, the Cac

Most of southeastern Alaska lies within the Alexander ter- rane (Figure 1), a 100-km-wide belt extending from the Yu- kon-Alaska border to the south tip of Prince of Wales Island [Berg et al., 1972, 1978]. The terrane consists of Ordovician through Triassic rocks that were deposited near a continental margin or possibly in an island arc. The Alexander terrane is separated from the west edge of the craton, defined as the Rocky Mountain trench, by several belts that include a belt of late Paleozoic oceanic crust. This oceanic terrane, the Cache Creek assemblage defined by Monger [1977], contains abun- dant chert, pillow basalt, and ultramafic rocks deposited in a deep ocean basin. Palcomagnetic evidence suggests that the Alexander terrane moved approximately 15 ø north sometime after the Carboniferous and thereby trapped the oceanic Cache Creek assemblage against the continent [Van der Voo et al., 1980]. The geologic history of southeastern Alaska is complicated by the presence of an outermost belt, Wrangellia, part of which lies west of the Alexander terrane on Chichagof and Baranof islands [Jones et al., 1977]. GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The Archaan greenstone sequence of the Pilbara craton is very diverse, containing most of the rock types found in other greenstone sequences of the world. A detailed description of the succession is given by Hickman and Lipple [1975]. The Warrawoona Group forms the basal, predominantly volcanic assemblage. Relatively thin chart units occur frequently inter- posed between ultramafic-mafic and ultramafic-felsic cycles. The upper part of the succession, the Gorge Creek Group, is predominantly a sedimentary assemblage of banded iron for- mations, argillaceous rocks, and sandstones with subordinate pillow basalt. The layered succession commonly exceeds 15 km in thickness and has been subjected to isoclinal folding. In the area sampled around Marble Bar (Figure 1) the beds are slightly overturned, as is clearly evidenced from the facing of the pillow basalts at the two localities. Greenschist facies metamorphism predominates in most areas. There have been two intervals of granite emplacement, a main one at around 3000 Ma [Campston and/trriens, 1968] and a younger event when the main granite batholiths were intruded by irregular masses of adamellite at around 2600 Ma. Generally, three components of magnetization were ob- served in both the red dacite and the pillow basalt when using either alternating field or thermal techniques. All samples usually contained a temporary component acquired during storage in the present geomagnetic field. In the red dacite there is a very resistant component preserved at fields of 200 roT, and thermal demagnetization analysis shows that this is a high-temperature component with blocking temperatures above 525øC and up to at least 640øC. This high-temperature, high-coercivity component is clearly from a hematite fraction. In these rocks, thermal demagnetization is often difficult at high temperatures because of the instability of the magnetite, which tends to oxidize. There is also an intermediate-temper- ature (250ø-500øC), intermediate-coercivity (10-40 mT) com- ponent that appears to be derived from the magnetite fraction. These components will be referred to as the H and M com- ponents, respectively (Figure 2). TABLE 2. Generally, three components of magnetization were ob- served in both the red dacite and the pillow basalt when using either alternating field or thermal techniques. All samples usually contained a temporary component acquired during storage in the present geomagnetic field. In the red dacite there is a very resistant component preserved at fields of 200 roT, and thermal demagnetization analysis shows that this is a high-temperature component with blocking temperatures above 525øC and up to at least 640øC. This high-temperature, high-coercivity component is clearly from a hematite fraction. In these rocks, thermal demagnetization is often difficult at high temperatures because of the instability of the magnetite, which tends to oxidize. There is also an intermediate-temper- ature (250ø-500øC), intermediate-coercivity (10-40 mT) com- ponent that appears to be derived from the magnetite fraction. These components will be referred to as the H and M com- ponents, respectively (Figure 2). TABLE 2. GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The Archaan greenstone sequence of the Pilbara craton is very diverse, containing most of the rock types found in other greenstone sequences of the world. A detailed description of the succession is given by Hickman and Lipple [1975]. The Warrawoona Group forms the basal, predominantly volcanic assemblage. Relatively thin chart units occur frequently inter- posed between ultramafic-mafic and ultramafic-felsic cycles. The upper part of the succession, the Gorge Creek Group, is predominantly a sedimentary assemblage of banded iron for- mations, argillaceous rocks, and sandstones with subordinate pillow basalt. The layered succession commonly exceeds 15 km in thickness and has been subjected to isoclinal folding. In the area sampled around Marble Bar (Figure 1) the beds are slightly overturned, as is clearly evidenced from the facing of the pillow basalts at the two localities. Greenschist facies metamorphism predominates in most areas. There have been two intervals of granite emplacement, a main one at around 3000 Ma [Campston and/trriens, 1968] and a younger event when the main granite batholiths were intruded by irregular masses of adamellite at around 2600 Ma. GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The Archaan greenstone sequence of the Pilbara craton is very diverse, containing most of the rock types found in other greenstone sequences of the world. A detailed description of the succession is given by Hickman and Lipple [1975]. The Warrawoona Group forms the basal, predominantly volcanic assemblage. Relatively thin chart units occur frequently inter- posed between ultramafic-mafic and ultramafic-felsic cycles. The upper part of the succession, the Gorge Creek Group, is predominantly a sedimentary assemblage of banded iron for- mations, argillaceous rocks, and sandstones with subordinate pillow basalt. The layered succession commonly exceeds 15 km in thickness and has been subjected to isoclinal folding. In the area sampled around Marble Bar (Figure 1) the beds are slightly overturned, as is clearly evidenced from the facing of the pillow basalts at the two localities. Greenschist facies metamorphism predominates in most areas. There have been two intervals of granite emplacement, a main one at around 3000 Ma [Campston and/trriens, 1968] and a younger event when the main granite batholiths were intruded by irregular masses of adamellite at around 2600 Ma. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: arolina 28403 A stable remanence was isolated from three groups of rocks collected in the Eastern Desert of Egypt. Two groups of dikes, one collected north of the Qena-Safaga road and the other about 200 km to the south near the Um Rus gold mine, gave paleomagnetic pole positions of 87øN, 304øE and 86øN, 185øE, respectively. Both have K/Ar ages in the range 480-530 m.y. The results are compatible with data re- ported from other Gondwana cratonic areas for this time period. The third group of rocks were samples of the Dokhan Volcanic Series collected at seven sites along the Qena-Safaga road. The paleomagnetic pole position of the higher-coercivity component, 36øS, 17øE, acquired about 600 m.y. ago is not easily reconciled with established polar wander paths. The younger component, however, with a paleomagnetic pole lying at 54øN, 327øE, suggests a Cambro-Ordovician age. Here a Precambrian succession extends virtually without break from latitude 30øN to the Sudanese border. To the west the Precambrian rocks plunge beneath the Cre- taceous arenaceous beds of the Nubian Formation. The east- ern margin of the Red Sea Hills is usually an unconformity between the Precambrian and the Mesozoic-Cenozoic, in some places Campanian-Maestrichtian or Paleocene-Eocene, in others Miocene. The existence of Precambrian rocks in the Red Sea Hills has been known for a long time, but despite the monumental efforts of Hume [1934, 1935] and more recently by Egyptian geologists [e.g., El $hazly, 1964], they have remained rela- tively poorly known, for the numbers working in this exten- sive but inhospitable terrain has remained small. The oldest known rocks so far recorded in the Eastern Desert are the migmatized gneisses from

geosynclinal volcanics, and the overlying Hammamat Formation contains primarily arena- ceous sediments of a postgeosynclinal phase. However, a Rb/ Sr isochron age of 603 m.y. obtained from the Dokhan Vol- canics by R. Stern (personal communication, 1979) suggests the lavas are coeval with the lower part of the Hammamat Copyright ¸ 1980 by the American Geophysical Union. arolina 28403 A stable remanence was isolated from three groups of rocks collected in the Eastern Desert of Egypt. Two groups of dikes, one collected north of the Qena-Safaga road and the other about 200 km to the south near the Um Rus gold mine, gave paleomagnetic pole positions of 87øN, 304øE and 86øN, 185øE, respectively. Both have K/Ar ages in the range 480-530 m.y. The results are compatible with data re- ported from other Gondwana cratonic areas for this time period. The third group of rocks were samples of the Dokhan Volcanic Series collected at seven sites along the Qena-Safaga road. The paleomagnetic pole position of the higher-coercivity component, 36øS, 17øE, acquired about 600 m.y. ago is not easily reconciled with established polar wander paths. The younger component, however, with a paleomagnetic pole lying at 54øN, 327øE, suggests a Cambro-Ordovician age. INTRODUCTION Although the Precambrian rocks of the Egyptian basement crop out in the Nile Valley and at Gebel Oweinat, the frontier region with the Sudan and the Libyan Arab Jamahariya, by far the most extensive outcrops occur in the Red Sea Hills (Figure 1). Here a Precambrian succession extends virtually without break from latitude 30øN to the Sudanese border. To the west the Precambrian rocks plunge bene

rphism. Whichever may be the case, it is clear that the rocks have been locally crushed, faulted, and tilted [Schiir- mann, 1966]. Akaad [1972] regards erosion of the rapidly up- lifted Dokhan Volcanic Formation as the source of the mate- rial found in the conglomeratic facies of the Hammamat Formation. Petrology. The rhyolitic, andesitic, and trachytic lavas and tuffs all show some degree of alteration. Some samples con- tain devitrified glass or a fine-grained groundmass with phenocrysts. The feldspars show the greatest degree of altera- tion with the development of a chlorite, some quartz, and epi- dote assemblage. Disseminated opaque minerals are abun- dant, sometimes exceeding 5%; however, the intensity of magnetization shows that they play little or no part in sample remanence. In reflected light a reddish color is general, often concentrated around grains or in veins. There is a consid- erable variation from sample to sample, from samples in which red (hematitic?) material obscures the general petrology to those in which alteration is less and original structures and minerals can be recognized. Paleomagnetic observations. A preliminary suite of sam- ples were collected from seven sites along the well exposed and most accessible section in the Dokhan Volcanic Forma-

of the columnar jointng. Detailed consideration of the petrology, geochemistry, and paleomagnetic behavior will appear in a subsequent report based upon current studies of a more complete sampling of the Qena-Safaga section and of exposures in Wadi Queh. Of the latter the dis- persion of the individual samples resulted in the elimination of site 3, which has an unacceptably high circle of confidence. INTRODUCTION Although the Precambrian rocks of the Egyptian basement crop out in the Nile Valley and at Gebel Oweinat, the frontier region with the Sudan and the Libyan Arab Jamahariya, by far the most extensive outcrops occur in the Red Sea Hills (Figure 1). Here a Precambrian succession extends virtually without break from latitude 30øN to the Sudanese border. To the west the Precambrian rocks plunge beneath the Cre- taceous arenaceous beds of the Nubian Formation. The east- ern margin of the Red Sea Hills is usually an unconformity between the Precambrian and the Mesozoic-Cenozoic, in some places Campanian-Maestrichtian or Paleocene-Eocene, in others Miocene.
